## Part 2: Topic and Data

### Context of the problem to be analyzed:

The problem to be analyzed is the relationship between the financial burden of higher education (specifically the ratio of financial aid to tuition costs) and student outcomes (specifically graduation rates). The analysis will test the assumption that a decrease in financial aid relative to tuition costs negatively impacts graduation rates, and that the COVID-19 pandemic likely exacerbated these negative effects.

This analysis is important for understanding equity and accessibility in U.S. higher education. By examining detailed breakdowns by race, gender, and institutional categories (like HBCUs or religious affiliations), the project can highlight how financial pressures disparately affect different demographic groups and institutional types.

The scope of this project covers U.S. colleges and universities using data from the past 10 years. The analysis will be national in scope, with the ability to filter data for any school in the country, allowing for detailed breakdowns by race and gender for each race, as well as by institutional characteristics.

The primary goal is to develop an application that allows users to visualize and explore these financial-to-outcome ratios. The analysis will specifically focus on visualizing 10-year trends and correlating the changes in aid-to-tuition ratios with corresponding changes in graduation rates.

### Literature Review:

#### 1:

Loeb, Susanna, and Marianne E. Page. "Examining the Link Between Teacher Wages and Student Outcomes: The Importance of Alternative Labor Market Opportunities and Non-Pecuniary Variation." *The Review of Economics and Statistics*, vol. 82, no. 3, Aug. 2000, pp. 393-408. *Stanford CEPA*, <https://cepa.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/loebpage.pdf>.

The relationship between a university’s resources and its students’ success is a cornerstone of educational research across the country. Intuitively, it may seem that increased spending should lead to better outcomes, but studies often struggle to find a consistent, systematic link. For instance, reviews of literature on this topic have shown that student outcomes are not consistently related to teacher salaries or per-pupil expenditures. This raises questions for analytics in higher education as to what specific factors truly drive student achievement if it is not raw financial input. A study by Susanna Loeb and Marianne E. Page, “Examining the Link Between Teacher Wages and Student Outcomes”, provides an interesting answer. The authors argue that previous research failed to produce robust results because they overlooked important economic and social variables. Specifically, they point out the importance of accounting for non-pecuniary job attributes, such as school safety and parental involvement, and alternative labor market opportunities for teachers. A high salary may not attract the best educators if other, more lucrative professions are readily available in the same geographic area.By creating a “relative wage” measure that compares teacher salaries to those of other college educated professionals, Loed and Page were able to isolate the true effect of compensation. Their findings were significant where after controlling for those external factors, they estimated that a 10% increase in teacher wages reduces high school dropout rates by 3% to 4%. This demonstrates that when salaries are competitive within the local labor market, they have a tangible positive impact on student retention. This study provides a strong theoretical framework for analyzing our dataset on U.S. universities and colleges. While Loed and Page focused on high schools, their methodology is directly applicable to higher education. By examining variables such as staff salaries, we can investigate whether universities that invest more in their faculty see higher graduation rates. Furthermore, this research encourages us to consider how institutional investment interacts with student preparedness, as indicated by things like SAT/ACT scores, to produce successful student outcomes. 

#### 2:

Heil, S., Reisel, L., & Attewell, P. (2014). College Selectivity and Degree Completion. American Educational Research Journal, 51(5), 913–935. <https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831214544298>

College Selectivity and Degree Completion, by Scott Heil, Liza Reisel, and Paul Attewell looked at if college selectivity affected a college student’s likelihood of graduation. This paper measured if a student were to graduate college within 6 years of starting, and used many predictors including SAT selectivity and tuition. They adjusted for likelihood of attending a college or a certain level and then compared how different predictors were associated with chances of graduation. They found graduation rates were largely affected by the makeup of the student body and by high tuition. They concluded that selectivity of a college does affect graduation rates to a very small extent, but that there is weak evidence that the chance of graduation for students who would struggle to graduate would improve if they attended a more selective college. Our project includes data on many US colleges and a big variable we are looking at is graduation numbers. It is helpful to know that selectivity of the school likely doesn’t play a key role in a student graduating, but it would be interesting to look at tuition in correlation to those graduation rates.

#### 3:

The study “The Impact of Tuition Increases on Enrollment at Public Colleges and Universities” by Steven W. Hemelt and Dave E. Marcotte (2011) provides foundational insight into how rising tuition costs affect student access and retention in higher education. Using data from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) from 1991 to 2006, the authors examined enrollment responses to changes in tuition across all U.S. public four-year institutions

### Proposed Data Source:

Our data comes from: <https://ies.ed.gov/> - Institute of Education Sciences

We pulled data from 2013-2023. The website allows for selection fromvarious data sets with various filters. We ended up with 5 different raw data sets that will later be cleaned and combined.

Characteristics data: 2208 rows, 11 columns; contains the school names and characteristics.

Enrollment data: 371882 rows, 6 columns; contains enrollment data of each college with different demographic data.

Financial aid data: 88321 rows, 6 columns; contains each college and relevant aid types and amounts.

Grad data: 677501 rows, 8 columns; contains number of graduated students in each college with a few demographics.

Tuition data: 495059 rows, 5 columns; contains both in and out of state tuition for each university.

## Part 3: Use Case

### Use Case & Actor Description

Our primary actors are prospective students and parents and researchers, either for institutions themselves or for policymaking. The prospective students and parents are motivated by a practical need to find the "best value" college; their goal is to use our app's demographic filters (race, gender) to see the 10-year aid-to-tuition ratios and graduation rates for students like them. The researchers are motivated by a research need; their goal is to use our app's institutional filters (e.g., HBCU, Public/Private) to identify systemic trends and use the statistical analysis features to find evidence for how financial aid correlate with student outcomes.

The app's workflow directly serves both actors' goals. The prospective students and parents will filter for a specific school and demographic, then visually compare the multi-year trend lines for the aid-to-tuition ratio and graduation rates to inform their enrollment decision. The researchers will take this one step further and after filtering for a group of institutions, they will click the "Run Statistical Analysis" button to quantify the visual trend. This provides them with a correlation coefficient and regression output, allowing them to statistically test the hypothesis that changes in financial aid are directly associated with changes in graduation rates for that institutional category

### Actor Questions of Interest

Our app could help users answer four key types of questions:

1.  **Data Look up:** What are the current tuition, average financial aid, and graduation rates at a specific school?

2.  **Trend Analysis:** How have these metrics (especially the aid-to-tuition ratio and graduation rates) changed over the last 10 years?

3.  **Equity Analysis:** How do these trends differ for specific groups based on race, gender, or institutional type (like HBCU or religious affiliation)?

4.  **Hypothesis Testing:** Is there a statistically significant correlation between the financial aid-to-tuition ratio and graduation rates for a given school or demographic?

### Anticipated Workflow for the Actor

1.  **Entry and Initial Selection:** The user lands on the application's main page. They are presented with a search bar to find a specific institution by name (e.g., "University of Alabama") and a set of primary categorical filters (e.g., State, Control of Institution: Public/Private, Historically Black College or University, Religious Affiliation).
2.  **Filtering and Data Loading:** The user either searches for a single school or selects a set of filters (e.g., "Public" and "HBCU"). Upon selection, the application queries the dataset and loads the relevant financial and outcome data.
3.  **Initial Visualization:** The user is shown a primary dashboard for their selection. This dashboard features a main line chart displaying two key trends over the past 10 years:
    -   **Metric 1:** The Aid-to-Tuition Ratio (calculated from `financial_aid_data.csv` and `tuition_data.csv`).

    -   **Metric 2:** The 6-Year Graduation Rate (calculated from `grad_data.csv` and `enrollment_data.csv`).
4.  **Demographics:** The user wants to see how these trends affect a specific subgroup so they use secondary filters on the dashboard to select a `Race` (e.g., "Black or African American") and `Gender` (e.g., "Women").
5.  **Data Refresh:** The visualizations instantly update so that the 10-year trend lines for both the aid ratio and graduation rate are recalculated to reflect the data only for Black or African American women at the selected institution(s).
6.  **Visual Insight:** The user visually inspects the two charts and forms a hypothesis. For example, they might observe, "It looks like when the aid ratio dipped between 2017 and 2019, the graduation rate for this group also leveled off or declined."
7.  **Statistical Analysis:** To test this visual hypothesis, the user clicks a button labeled **"Run Statistical Analysis."**
8.  **Model Results Display:** The application runs a correlation test and a simple linear regression on the 10 data points displayed in the charts (the 10 yearly values for Aid Ratio vs. Grad Rate). A new "Analysis" card appears on the dashboard with a plain-English summary:
    -   **Correlation Coefficient: r = #.## (Moderately Strong Positive)**

    -   **Interpretation:** "This suggests a positive relationship. For this group, years with higher aid-to-tuition ratios were also associated with higher graduation rates."

    -   **Regression Model:** "For every #% increase in the aid-to-tuition ratio, the graduation rate was associated with a **#.## percentage point increase**."

    -   **Model Fit (R-squared): #.##**("This means ##% of the change in graduation rates over this 10-year period can be statistically explained by the changes in the aid-to-tuition ratio.")
9.  **Drawing Insights:** The actor can now make a much stronger conclusion. They have combined their visual observation with a quantitative, statistical test, allowing them to confirm or not confirm their assumption (that less aid hurts grad rates) with statistical evidence for the specific school and demographic they are investigating.

## Part 5: App Concept

### Layout of the App

Our application will be designed as a single-page, interactive dashboard. We decided to have a single page design to make the user's workflow more seamless and make the connection between the visual trends and statistical analysis clear. The UI will be divided into two main sections: a persistent Control Panel on the left and a dynamic Dashboard Display on the right.

**1. Left Sidebar: Control Panel**

This panel serves as the user's primary starting point for all queries. It will contain all the controls needed to select a dataset for analysis.

-   **School Search Bar:** A text search field allowing the user to find and select a specific institution by name.

-   **Primary Institutional Filters:** A set of dropdown menus to filter for groups of schools. Filters will include:

    -   Control of Institution (Public, Private not-for-profit, etc.)

    -   State

    -   Historically Black College or University (Yes/No)

    -   Religious Affiliation

    -   Degree of Urbanization (City, Suburb, etc.)

-   **Year Selection:** A set of check boxes to allow the user to customize the years used in the data selection.

**2. Main Area: Dashboard Display**

This section is the dynamic output area where all visualizations and analysis are displayed. It will update based on the user's selections.

-   **Demographic Filter Bar:** Located at the top of the main area, this bar will contain dropdowns for Race and Gender, allowing the user to drill down into the data. These filters will update the visualizations in real-time.

-   **Main Trend Visualization:** This will be the largest component on the screen—an interactive line chart showing the selected year trends for the selected school(s) and demographic.

    -   **Interactivity:** The user can hover over any point on the lines to see a tooltip with the exact values for that year.

-   **Statistical Analysis Card:** This section will be positioned directly below the main chart to provide immediate, contextual analysis.

    -   **"Run Statistical Analysis" Button:** When clicked, this will run the correlation and regression models on the currently displayed data.

    -   **Results Display:** A card will appear with a plain-English summary of the results, including the Correlation Coefficient, the Linear Regression Summary (e.g., "A 1% increase in aid ratio was associated with a 0.35 point increase in grad rate"), and the R-Squared value.

-   **Data table viewer:**

    -   At the bottom of the layout, we will add a interactive data table viewer to allow users to see the data for themselves.

### User Data Selection and Manipulation

A user will have the option to search for specific institutions to select data, or filter data by year or other categories based on our categorical variables (such as public/private university) and see the resulting data set.

We will also provide the option to log certain numerical columns for future use visualization use.

### Approach to Team Workflow, collaboration and branching

Our group will use a coordinated approach centered on GitHub for version control and a dedicated message channel for daily communication. We will follow a simplified branching model where the `main` branch is protected and stores only stable, milestone-ready versions. Each team member will conduct all development on their own persistent, personal branch, named after them. When a task or feature is complete, the group member will submit a Pull Request on GitHub to merge their personal branch into the `main` branch. This Pull Request will require review and approval from at least one other group member to ensure code quality, share knowledge, and prevent conflicts. This workflow allows us to work in parallel on our individual branches while ensuring the `main` branch always remains in a functional state. To further avoid merge conflicts, we have implemented a system in a shared doc that allows us to see which part of the project someone is currently working on. This way, two group members will not be overwriting each others code with their work at the same time.
